detail.body:
Co-authored with @Shunkangz and @mohammedabdulwahhab.

## Motivation

The weight cache daemon (#27139) shares weights with engines through `torch_ipc`, which uses CUDA IPC handles. The `vmm_fd` backend in `weight_cache/transport.py` is still a placeholder that raises `NotImplementedError`; #33522 and #27310 (§4.2, phase 1) both plan it.

With CUDA VMM, the engine reserves its own virtual address range and maps the daemon's allocations into it. With `cudaIpcOpenMemHandle`, the caller cannot choose the address. That difference gives:

1. **In this PR:** a daemon exit no longer kills the engine. CUDA frees a `cuMemCreate` allocation only after every mapping and handle to it is released, so an attached engine keeps valid weights, and the SIGKILL watchdog is only needed for `torch_ipc`.
2. **Follow-ups:** release the weights and map them back later at the same addresses, so that pointers captured in CUDA graphs stay valid. This would allow weight release/resume with the cache on (rejected today by `_assert_weight_cache_inactive`), the roadmap's epoch handoff, and engine snapshots that re-attach the node's resident weights instead of reading them from the checkpoint (#43965, #40736; a proposed design, not tested here). In this PR the engine maps once and does not re-map.

The KV cache needs no new transport: with `--enable-memory-saver`, torch_memory_saver already allocates it with CUDA VMM and keeps its addresses across pause and resume.

## Modifications

- `--weight-cache-transport {auto,torch_ipc,vmm_fd}`, the flag named in #33522. On the daemon, `auto` keeps `torch_ipc` for now; on an engine, `auto` accepts whatever the daemon serves, while a named transport refuses a daemon serving the other.
- Daemon: after loading, pack each rank's tensors into a few large exportable allocations (new `weight_cache/vmm_layout.py`), freeing each original as it goes. Aliases and tied weights keep sharing storage.
- Protocol: `fetch_state` sends the layout, then one fd per allocation over `SCM_RIGHTS`. `_recv_fd` takes every delivered fd before any check, closes them on error, refuses truncated ancillary data and uses `MSG_CMSG_CLOEXEC`.
- Engine: reserve one address range, import and map each allocation, and pass the tensors to the existing `_set_module_tensor` path. Mappings are kept until the process exits, because a parameter can outlive the model object.
- With `vmm_fd`, a daemon exit is logged and the engine keeps serving. The watchdog stays for `torch_ipc`.
- `preloaded_weights_bytes` reports the packed allocations. `expandable_segments` is allowed in a `vmm_fd` daemon.
- `IpcModelLoader` is renamed to `WeightCacheModelLoader`, since it now serves both transports. The module name `ipc_loader.py`, the internal `ipc_cache` load format and the "Loaded model via IPC" log text stay as they are.
- Tests: CPU unit tests in `test_weight_cache_vmm_fd.py`, and a `vmm_fd` variant of each of the five GPU test classes in `test_weight_cache_daemon.py`.

Not done yet: loading straight into exportable memory, read-only mappings, docs, and in-tree byte-level parity checks.

Follow-ups, in separate PRs: release and re-attach the weights at the same addresses; the epoch handoff (#33522); release and re-attach the KV cache together with the weights; refresh PD KV-transfer registrations after a re-attach; engine snapshots (#43965 / #40736).

## Accuracy Tests

On B200 GPUs, with a recent nightly image. The GPU runs below were made on earlier revisions of this change; after the rebase onto the current `main`, only the CPU tests and lint were rerun.

- **In-tree:** the 37 tests that cover the five `vmm_fd` variants and the `torch_ipc` classes they compare with pass. The two parent MoE classes fail at setup on SM100 under `torch_ipc` as well (see Known limitations).
- **Manual parity runs:** Qwen3-0.6B TP1, TP2, TP8 and PP2; Qwen3-0.6B-FP8 (block-wise) TP2; Qwen3-30B-A3B TP8, TP8+EP8, and TP8 across two nodes; a TP2 daemon with `expandable_segments`; Qwen3.5-0.8B; Falcon-H1-0.5B-Instruct with CUDA graphs off (with them on, it crashed even when loading from disk in our image).
  - Weights: for every parameter and buffer on every rank, `vmm_fd` matches disk and `torch_ipc` in shape, dtype, stride, storage offset/size and SHA-256 hashes; alias groups are kept.
  - Greedy tokens (8 prompts x 32 tokens) are identical on all three servers, and stay the same after the `vmm_fd` daemon is killed with SIGKILL.
  - A probe process (not run for PP2 and the two hybrid models) found no fd leaks, and every imported tensor lies inside the reserved range.
- **GSM8K**, all 1319 questions, 5-shot; the disk server ran twice to show run-to-run variation:

| Configuration | disk | disk, second pass | `torch_ipc` | `vmm_fd` | `vmm_fd` after the daemon kill |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-0.6B, TP8 | 0.390 | 0.391 | 0.390 | 0.390 | 0.393 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B, TP8 | 0.911 | 0.909 | 0.909 | 0.912 | 0.909 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B, TP8 + EP8 | 0.905 | 0.904 | 0.904 | 0.907 | 0.907 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B, TP8 over two nodes | 0.910 | 0.911 | 0.916 | 0.903 | 0.905 |
| Qwen3-0.6B-FP8 (block-wise FP8), TP2 | 0.396 | 0.396 | 0.396 | 0.396 | 0.396 |
| Qwen3-0.6B, TP2, `expandable_segments` daemon | 0.390 | 0.390 | 0.390 | 0.390 | 0.390 |
| Qwen3-0.6B, PP2 | 0.382 | 0.382 | 0.381 | 0.382 | 0.381 |
| Qwen3.5-0.8B, TP1 | 0.332 | 0.332 | 0.332 | 0.332 | 0.332 |
| Falcon-H1-0.5B, TP1, no CUDA graphs | 0.722 | 0.724 | 0.723 | 0.717 | 0.725 |

- **Serving** (Qwen3-30B-A3B TP2 unless noted):
  - MMLU: 925 of 1140 on disk, `torch_ipc` and `vmm_fd`.
  - With both daemons resident, the `vmm_fd` engine's KV cache size matches the `torch_ipc` engine's within tolerance.
  - 20 client-mode restarts (Qwen3-0.6B TP2) return the disk server's tokens, with no daemon fd or GPU memory growth.
  - `--weight-cache-mode daemon` works (Qwen3-0.6B TP2).
  - A 30-minute soak shows no GPU memory growth and no errors.

Most runs predate the mapping-lifetime and fd-receive changes. With those changes, the in-tree tests, FP8 and `expandable_segments` runs, six client-mode restarts, daemon mode and a 15-minute soak were rerun successfully.

Not tested: Mamba-type models with CUDA graphs on, MoE runner backends other than `triton`, expert parallelism with an all-to-all backend, and GPUs other than B200.

## Known limitations

- POSIX file descriptors only, so the engine and the daemon must be on the same node. ROCm stays on `torch_ipc`.
- The existing quantization allowlist (unquantized and block-wise FP8) applies to both transports.
- Export fails if a model tensor is not on this GPU, for example a CPU buffer. `torch_ipc` handles that.
- As with `torch_ipc`, objects that the model derives after loading and keeps as plain attributes are not exported, for example DeepSeek MLA's `w_kc` / `w_vc` (from reading the code). A tensor that is still referenced outside the parameters and buffers stays alive in the daemon as an extra copy.
- Mappings stay until the process exits. SGLang does not load a second model with the cache on, because weight updates are refused.
- The shared weights are writable: an in-place write in one engine changes every engine's copy. EPLB rebalancing does this, for `torch_ipc` too; #45341 addresses it. The EP tests here never rebalance.
- On SM100, DeepGEMM's UE8M0 repack of block-FP8 scales and BF16 Qwen3-MoE's default `flashinfer_trtllm` runner change weights after loading, which a meta-initialized engine cannot reproduce. This affects `torch_ipc` too. The runs above used `SGLANG_ENABLE_JIT_DEEPGEMM=0` for FP8 and `--moe-runner-backend triton` for MoE. `CacheConfig` does not record the MoE runner, so the daemons and the engine must use the same one.
- Mixed builds (from reading the code): an engine from before this PR fails against a `vmm_fd` daemon, without falling back to disk. Upgrade daemons and engines together, and keep `auto` while a node runs both builds.

## Related

- #27139 (the daemon), #33279 (the transport abstraction with the `vmm_fd` placeholder), #33522 (the roadmap), #27310 §4.2 (the same change, proposed as phase 1), #39091 (CUDA graph serialization, which needs stable weight addresses).
- ishandhanani/sglang#14 and hutm/sglang#13 implement the same transport on forks.
- Found along the way: #45341 (the daemon keeps the EPLB expert layout) and #45363 (load all local replicas of each expert).
- Adjacent, with their scope unchanged: #36293, #37459, #36156, #44241.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not measured yet: weight import time, `vmm_fd` vs `torch_ipc`.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [ ] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

## Review and Merge Process

1. Ping Merge Oncalls to start the process. See the [PR Merge Process](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.github/MAINTAINER.md#pull-request-merge-process).
2. Get approvals from [CODEOWNERS](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.github/CODEOWNERS) and other reviewers.
3. Trigger CI tests with [comments](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#how-to-trigger-ci-tests) or contact authorized users to do so.
   - Common commands include `/tag-and-rerun-ci`, `/tag-run-ci-label`, `/rerun-failed-ci`
4. After green CI and required approvals, ask Merge Oncalls or people with Write permission to merge the PR.

+"""Packing layout for the ``vmm_fd`` weight cache transport.
+
+The daemon copies its final tensors into a few large CUDA VMM allocations and
+the engine maps those allocations into its own address space. Every distinct

+allocation. A tensor is described relative to its slot the same way torch
+describes it relative to its storage (``storage_offset``, ``shape``,

+transposes, slices, dtype views) share one storage again in the engine.

+SLOT_ALIGNMENT = 512

+class TestAttachAfterAFailedAttach(CustomTestCase):
+    """A client that breaks off a fetch_state part-way leaves the daemon able
+    to serve the next one: every fd exported or received for the broken
+    request is closed, the daemon keeps its allocation handles, and the next
+    client gets fresh fds for them and reads every tensor.

+    does; memfds and host memory stand in for the driver's fd export and the
+    engine's mapping, so the handles here are placeholders (the GPU tests map
+    real allocations). Both sides run in this process, so the fd count covers
+    both."""
+
+    # Where the client gives up, in the order of the exchange.
+    BREAK_OFF_POINTS = (
+        "after_request",  # before the daemon answers: its send fails
+        "after_response",  # whatever fds were sent are left on the socket
+        "midway_through_fds",  # the daemon's send fails after half of them
+        "mapping_fails",  # after every fd arrived
+        "after_mapping",  # without importing any tensor
+    )
+    # The daemon's send fails at these points; at the others it may finish.
+    DAEMON_SEND_FAILS = ("after_request", "midway_through_fds")

+        model = _TinyModel()
+        tensors = dict(model.named_parameters(remove_duplicate=False))
+        tensors.update(model.named_buffers(remove_duplicate=False))
+        self.expected = {name: t.detach().clone() for name, t in tensors.items()}
+        del tensors

+        backend = VmmFdTransportBackend(
+            device=CPU, granularity=GRANULARITY, max_alloc_bytes=SLOT_ALIGNMENT
+        )

+    def _serve(self, conn, errors):
+        """Handle one connection in a thread, as WeightCacheDaemon.serve() does."""
+
+        def handle():
+            try:
+                self.daemon._handle_connection(conn)
+            except Exception as e:  # serve() logs it and goes on
+                errors.append(e)
+            finally:
+                conn.close()

+        thread = threading.Thread(target=handle)
+        thread.start()
+        return thread

+        ``break_off``. Returns copies of every tensor the client imported
+        (None if it gave up) and the errors the daemon raised."""
+        daemon_sock, client_sock = socket.socketpair()
+        for sock in (daemon_sock, client_sock):

**Loading approach**

What drove the choice to load normally and relocate the final weights, rather than using a custom MemPool that directly loads into VMM backing? 

From reading this change, it seems re-location is quite an involved technique requiring a correct impl across the following concerns:
- Correctly (and efficiently) packing tensor storages
- Correctly determining allocation granularity/alignments for the planned layout.
- Free-ing references to old storage tensors (from the ordinary allocator) so they are reclaimed
- Re-wiring model tensors to point to the new storage. Handling views, aliases, and other special cases.

It seems that we have it working for now, but I'd like to seriously vet the alternative (directly loading into VMM backing using a [CudaPluggableAllocator](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.15/generated/torch.cuda.memory.CUDAPluggableAllocator.html)) to see if we avoid implementing some of these concerns.

+"""Packing layout for the ``vmm_fd`` weight cache transport.
+
+The daemon copies its final tensors into a few large CUDA VMM allocations and
+the engine maps those allocations into its own address space. Every distinct
+storage becomes one *slot*: a byte range at an aligned offset inside one
+allocation. A tensor is described relative to its slot the same way torch
+describes it relative to its storage (``storage_offset``, ``shape``,
+``stride``), so tensors that shared a storage in the daemon (tied weights,
+transposes, slices, dtype views) share one storage again in the engine.

Thanks for raising this. We compared relocation with our own allocate-at-load prototype (a torch `MemPool` backed by a `CUDAPluggableAllocator` that creates one POSIX-fd-exportable VMM allocation per segment) on GLM-5.2-FP8 (TP8, 8x B200) and Qwen3-30B-A3B (TP8).

**What we measured**

- The prototype exports one VMM allocation per caching-allocator segment containing exported storage: 362 per rank on GLM-5.2 versus 151 with relocation (125 versus 8 on Qwen3-30B). Each attach sends one fd per allocation, which the client imports and maps. Median per-rank attach (fetch, import and map, rebuild the tensors; not a full engine start) is 0.57 s with relocation versus 1.0 s with the prototype, or 0.23 s versus 0.54 s with cached fds (28 ms versus 386 ms on Qwen3-30B).
- On GLM-5.2, the unpruned pool also keeps 0.57 GiB per GPU in allocations that hold no exported storage, plus 0.27 GiB outside the exported storages inside exported allocations. `preloaded_weights_bytes` is 89.3 GiB per GPU versus 88.8 GiB with relocation.
- Relocation pays once per daemon load: about 0.22 s of packing per rank on GLM-5.2, and about 1.01 GiB of extra memory per GPU at the 1 GiB cap.

**On the concerns you listed**

- *Packing and granularity/alignment*: `vmm_layout.py` puts shared or overlapping storages in one slot, aligns slots to 512 bytes, and rounds allocations to the driver's granularity; the CPU tests cover these cases. Allocate-at-load skips the packing but still rounds every allocation to the granularity.
- *Freeing old storages*: the plan keeps tensor names, not tensors, and each copied tensor is repointed before the next allocation; `empty_cache()` then returns the segments that are fully free. That is where the transient above comes from. After the pack, no copied original was still live (rank-0 allocator trace).
- *Re-wiring, views and aliases*: in this version, repointing the model's tensors is what releases the originals during packing. Views and aliases share one slot, and each tensor's dtype, shape, stride and offset are sent; the client needs that metadata under either approach.

+# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
+"""Packing layout for the ``vmm_fd`` weight cache transport.
+
+The daemon copies its final tensors into a few large CUDA VMM allocations and
+the engine maps those allocations into its own address space. Every distinct
+storage becomes one *slot*: a byte range at an aligned offset inside one
+allocation. A tensor is described relative to its slot the same way torch
+describes it relative to its storage (``storage_offset``, ``shape``,
+``stride``), so tensors that shared a storage in the daemon (tied weights,
+transposes, slices, dtype views) share one storage again in the engine.
+
+Nothing here calls CUDA: planning, validation and rebuilding tensors only use
+torch metadata, so this module is unit-tested on CPU.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import bisect
+import dataclasses
+from typing import Any, Dict, List, Mapping, Sequence, Tuple
+
+import torch
+
+# The CUDA caching allocator hands out blocks aligned to 512 bytes. Slots use
+# the same alignment, so a packed tensor keeps the alignment it was loaded with.
+SLOT_ALIGNMENT = 512
+
+
+@dataclasses.dataclass
+class VmmSlot:
+    """One packed storage: ``nbytes`` at ``offset`` in allocation ``alloc_index``."""
+
+    alloc_index: int
+    offset: int
+    nbytes: int
+    # (name of a tensor on the source storage, byte offset of that storage in
+    # the slot, storage nbytes). More than one source only when distinct
+    # storages overlapped in the daemon.
+    sources: List[Tuple[str, int, int]]
+    # Every tensor that views this slot.
+    names: List[str]
+
+
+@dataclasses.dataclass
+class VmmPackPlan:
+    alloc_sizes: List[int]
+    slots: List[VmmSlot]
+    # Wire layout: one dict per tensor name, see plan_vmm_pack().
+    entries: Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]]
+
+
+def _align_up(value: int, alignment: int) -> int:
+    return (value + alignment - 1) // alignment * alignment
+
+
+def _is_int(value: Any) -> bool:
+    return isinstance(value, int) and not isinstance(value, bool)
+
+
+def parse_dtype(name: str) -> torch.dtype:
+    dtype = getattr(torch, name, None) if isinstance(name, str) else None
+    if not isinstance(dtype, torch.dtype):
+        raise ValueError(f"unknown dtype {name!r}")
+    return dtype
+
+
+def view_nbytes(
+    shape: Sequence[int], stride: Sequence[int], storage_offset: int, itemsize: int
+) -> int:
+    """Bytes a view needs from the start of its storage (0 for an empty view,
+    matching torch's own bounds check)."""
+    if any(size == 0 for size in shape):
+        return 0

+def plan_vmm_pack(
+    state_tensors: Mapping[str, Tuple[torch.Tensor, bool]],
+    *,
+    device: torch.device,
+    granularity: int,
+    max_alloc_bytes: int,
+) -> VmmPackPlan:
+    """Assign the storage behind every tensor in ``state_tensors`` to a slot.
+
+    Storages whose byte ranges overlap share one slot, so aliasing between
+    distinct storages survives too. Slots are placed in first-use order at
+    ``SLOT_ALIGNMENT``-aligned offsets. An allocation is closed when the next
+    slot would push it past ``max_alloc_bytes``; a larger storage gets an
+    allocation of its own. Allocation sizes are rounded up to ``granularity``.
+
+    Each entry holds ``alloc_index``, ``offset`` (slot start, bytes),
+    ``storage_nbytes`` (slot size), ``storage_offset`` (elements, relative to
+    the slot), ``shape``, ``stride``, ``dtype`` and ``is_param``. The plan
+    keeps tensor names, not tensors, so it does not keep any original alive.
+    """
+    if granularity <= 0 or granularity % SLOT_ALIGNMENT:
+        raise ValueError(
+            f"granularity {granularity} must be a positive multiple of {SLOT_ALIGNMENT}"
+        )
+    if max_alloc_bytes <= 0:
+        raise ValueError(f"max_alloc_bytes must be positive, got {max_alloc_bytes}")
+
+    # Storage span (start pointer, nbytes) behind every tensor. Empty storages
+    # get a zero-byte slot each.
+    tensor_spans: Dict[str, Tuple[int, int]] = {}
+    span_first_use: Dict[int, int] = {}  # start -> index of the first tensor
+    # start -> (nbytes, name): the largest storage at that start is the one
+    # copied, as it covers every smaller storage that starts there too.
+    span_source: Dict[int, Tuple[int, str]] = {}
+    empty_names: List[Tuple[int, str]] = []
+    for index, (name, (tensor, _)) in enumerate(state_tensors.items()):
+        if tensor.device != device:
+            raise ValueError(
+                f"tensor {name!r} is on {tensor.device}, expected {device}"
+            )
+        storage = tensor.untyped_storage()
+        start, nbytes = storage.data_ptr(), storage.nbytes()
+        tensor_spans[name] = (start, nbytes)
+        if nbytes == 0:
+            empty_names.append((index, name))
+            continue
+        span_first_use.setdefault(start, index)
+        if nbytes > span_source.get(start, (0, ""))[0]:
+            span_source[start] = (nbytes, name)
+
+    # Merge spans that overlap (spans that only touch stay separate).
+    span_starts = sorted(span_source)
+    groups: List[List[int]] = []  # [start, end, first_use]
+    for start in span_starts:
+        end = start + span_source[start][0]
+        if groups and start < groups[-1][1]:
+            groups[-1][1] = max(groups[-1][1], end)
+            groups[-1][2] = min(groups[-1][2], span_first_use[start])
+        else:
+            groups.append([start, end, span_first_use[start]])
+    group_starts = [group[0] for group in groups]
+
+    group_slots = [
+        VmmSlot(alloc_index=-1, offset=-1, nbytes=end - start, sources=[], names=[])
+        for start, end, _ in groups
+    ]
+    for start in span_starts:
+        group = bisect.bisect_right(group_starts, start) - 1
+        nbytes, name = span_source[start]
+        group_slots[group].sources.append((name, start - group_starts[group], nbytes))
+
+    tensor_slot: Dict[str, Tuple[VmmSlot, int]] = {}  # name -> (slot, byte offset)
+    for name, (start, nbytes) in tensor_spans.items():
+        if nbytes == 0:
+            continue
+        group = bisect.bisect_right(group_starts, start) - 1
+        group_slots[group].names.append(name)
+        tensor_slot[name] = (group_slots[group], start - group_starts[group])
+
+    ordered: List[Tuple[int, VmmSlot]] = [
+        (groups[i][2], slot) for i, slot in enumerate(group_slots)
+    ]
+    for index, name in empty_names:
+        slot = VmmSlot(alloc_index=-1, offset=-1, nbytes=0, sources=[], names=[name])
+        ordered.append((index, slot))
+        tensor_slot[name] = (slot, 0)
+    ordered.sort(key=lambda item: item[0])
+    slots = [slot for _, slot in ordered]
+
+    # Lay the slots out back to back, opening a new allocation when needed.
+    alloc_used: List[int] = []
+    for slot in slots:
+        offset = _align_up(alloc_used[-1], SLOT_ALIGNMENT) if alloc_used else 0
+        if not alloc_used or (
+            alloc_used[-1] > 0 and offset + slot.nbytes > max_alloc_bytes
+        ):
+            alloc_used.append(0)
+            offset = 0
+        slot.alloc_index = len(alloc_used) - 1
+        slot.offset = offset
+        alloc_used[-1] = offset + slot.nbytes
+    alloc_sizes = [_align_up(max(used, 1), granularity) for used in alloc_used]
+
+    entries: Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]] = {}
+    for name, (tensor, is_param) in state_tensors.items():
+        slot, byte_offset = tensor_slot[name]
+        itemsize = tensor.element_size()
+        if byte_offset % itemsize:
+            raise ValueError(
+                f"tensor {name!r} starts {byte_offset} bytes into a storage it "
+                f"overlaps with, which is not a multiple of its {itemsize}-byte "
+                f"element size"
+            )
+        entries[name] = {

You were right: the cap is not a peak-memory bound, and a storage can exceed it. The exact planned allocation sizes are known after loading, before packing starts, though:

- Packing fills one allocation at a time, drops its references to the copied originals, then synchronizes and calls `empty_cache()` before the next allocation. The extra memory includes the allocation being filled, cumulative layout padding, and copied originals Torch cannot return yet: ones still referenced elsewhere, or sharing an allocator segment with live tensors.
- A slot above the cap gets its own granularity-rounded allocation. In the five big MoE checkpoints measured at TP8, the largest slot, a layer's fused expert `w13_weight`, was at most 1 GiB per GPU: 1.00 GiB on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, 0.88 on DeepSeek-R1-0528, 0.75 on GLM-5.2-FP8, 0.59 on GLM-4.7 and 0.56 on GLM-5.3-Flash.

34ad349003 drops the "about one allocation" claim. Instead, 74d54c4f37 logs the largest slot and allocation before the first packing allocation, and 53ecd011d5 logs free device memory with them and warns when it is below the largest allocation. In the runs below, packing added almost the same memory as that largest allocation. If packing does fail, startup aborts before any engine can attach, so partially packed weights are never served. Read through the transport and layout code end to end — this is careful work. The fd discipline is exactly right (CLOEXEC on receive, MSG_CTRUNC refusal, close-before-raise on every error path, fresh export per fetch, import→map→release-handle on the engine), and the layout validation before any mapping plus the alias-preserving slot merge in `vmm_layout` cover the cases that usually bite in this kind of code. Deliberately retaining `_LOADED_MODEL_TRANSPORTS` for the process lifetime is the safe call for tensors that can outlive the model object.

Context for why we're reading closely: we maintain a hot-swap extension that tears down and re-captures CUDA graphs in a live server (#44284 came out of that work), so the follow-up you list — release and re-attach weights at the same addresses so pointers captured in CUDA graphs stay valid — is precisely the mechanism we've been looking for. Following #33522 for the epoch-handoff coordination.

We can add sm90 coverage: your GPU runs were on B200; we have H20 nodes and can run the five `vmm_fd` GPU test classes plus a manual parity pass (disk vs `torch_ipc` vs `vmm_fd` greedy tokens, daemon SIGKILL survival) against this branch on the v0.5.22 image. Will report results here.
